title: break and continue in Loops
learningObjectives: Explain the key idea in break and continue in loops.
Identify the relevant syntax and rules.
Trace each example and predict the result.
Apply the concept in a small program.
Avoid a common mistake related to this topic.

understand.concept: break exits the nearest enclosing loop immediately. continue skips the rest of the current iteration and proceeds to the next iteration. Both change control flow, so use them where they improve clarity.
understand.whyItMatters: These statements help stop searches early or skip values that do not need processing.
understand.analogy: Think of this as a control or calculation rule that tells a program how to handle a particular situation consistently.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is only a starting point; C++ syntax, types and execution rules determine actual behaviour.
understand.explain:
## break
Use break when a loop's work is complete or a stopping condition has been found.

## continue
Use continue to skip an iteration's remaining body statements while allowing the loop to continue.

## Readability
Avoid unnecessary control-flow jumps. Keep loop termination and updates easy to reason about, especially when continue occurs before an update in a while loop.

examples.title: Early exit
examples.code: for (int i{1}; i <= 5; ++i) { if (i == 3) break; std::cout << i << ' '; }
examples.explanation: The loop stops when i reaches 3.

examples.title: Skip odd values
examples.code: for (int i{1}; i <= 5; ++i) { if (i % 2 != 0) continue; std::cout << i << ' '; }
examples.explanation: Only even values reach the output statement.

examples.title: Search pattern
examples.code: int target{4};\nfor (int n : {2,4,6}) { if (n == target) { std::cout << "found"; break; } }
examples.explanation: break stops the search once the target is found.

examples.title: Continue in while safely
examples.code: int i{0};\nwhile (i < 4) { ++i; if (i == 2) continue; std::cout << i << ' '; }
examples.explanation: The counter is updated before continue, so the loop still progresses.

examples.title: Avoid nested loop confusion
examples.code: for (int row{0}; row < 2; ++row) { for (int col{0}; col < 3; ++col) { if (col == 1) continue; std::cout << row << col << ' '; } }
examples.explanation: continue affects the nearest enclosing loop only.
